# The Weight Behind the Lens

Kai is eighteen years old, slight-framed and quiet, with the kind of stillness about him that people sometimes mistake for calm. He sits in the therapy room with his camera bag resting against his leg, one hand occasionally dropping to touch it, as though confirming it is still there. He grew up in a small province in the Philippines, the eldest son of a family that needed him to be useful early. He was seventeen when he joined a paramilitary unit operating in a region where armed conflict had been grinding on for years longer than he had been alive. He told himself it would be temporary. He told himself he was ready.

He was not ready.

The incident that broke something open in him happened during a clearing operation in a village that was supposed to be empty. Kai was moving with his unit through a narrow lane between concrete walls when the shooting started. He describes it now in fragments — the sound arriving before he understood what it was, the man beside him dropping, the way time seemed to compress and then stretch in the same moment. He fired his weapon. He does not know with certainty what he hit. What he does know is that when the shooting stopped, he found a boy — perhaps twelve or thirteen years old — lying in the dirt near a doorway, and that the boy was looking at him when he died. Kai stood there for what felt like a very long time. His unit commander pulled him away.

Three weeks later, Kai was discharged on medical grounds after he stopped being able to function. He came to Manila to live with an aunt. He brought almost nothing with him except an old film camera his father had given him years before, and it is photography that has become both his refuge and his torment.

During the day, Kai moves through the city with his camera, shooting street scenes, markets, children playing near drainage canals. When he is behind the lens, there are moments — brief, unreliable — when the world narrows to something he can frame and hold. But the relief never lasts. He cannot photograph faces. When he tries, his hands begin to shake and his vision seems to tunnel, and he has to lower the camera and find somewhere to sit until the feeling passes. He has deleted hundreds of images of strangers' faces without being able to explain to himself why looking at them feels like standing again in that lane.

He sleeps badly and briefly. Most nights he is awake by two or three in the morning, lying rigid in the dark, listening to sounds he cannot always identify as real. He has a recurring dream in which he is trying to take a photograph of something important but the shutter will not release, and when he looks through the viewfinder there is only the boy's face, very close, very still. He wakes from this dream already sitting upright, heart slamming, drenched in sweat, and it takes him a long time to locate himself in his aunt's apartment.

He has stopped going to places that are crowded or loud. A market he once loved to photograph now feels impossible — the noise, the press of bodies, the sudden movements at the edges of his vision. He startled so violently at a motorbike backfiring last month that he knocked over a vendor's display and then could not stop shaking for an hour afterward. He was ashamed of this. He is ashamed of most of what he feels.

What Kai says he wants, when asked, is to be able to take portraits again. He says this carefully, looking at the camera bag rather than at the therapist. He means something larger than photography, though he does not yet have the language for it — he wants to be able to look at a face and see a person, rather than the last face he saw in that village, looking back at him.
